<p id="mwog"><b id="mwow">Python</b> is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-level_programming_language" title="High-level programming language" id="mwpA">high-level</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_programming_language" title="General-purpose programming language" id="mwpQ">general-purpose programming language</a> that emphasizes <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_readability" title="Code readability" class="mw-redirect" id="mwpg">code readability</a>, simplicity, and ease-of-writing with the use of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Significant_indentation" title="Significant indentation" class="mw-redirect" id="mwpw">significant indentation</a>,<sup about="#mwt183" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-7_40-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-7"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-7-40" id="mwqA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwqQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwqg">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwqw">]</span></span></a></sup> an extensive ("batteries-included") <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_library" title="Standard library" id="mwrA">standard library</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)" title="Garbage collection (computer science)" id="mwrQ">garbage collection</a>. Python supports multiple <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_paradigm" title="Programming paradigm" id="mwrg">programming paradigms</a> but with an emphasis on <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming" title="Object-oriented programming" id="mwrw">object-oriented programming</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_typing" title="Dynamic typing" class="mw-redirect" id="mwsA">dynamic typing</a>.</p>

<p id="mwsQ"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_van_Rossum" title="Guido van Rossum" id="mwsg">Guido van Rossum</a> began working on Python in the late 1980s as a successor to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_(programming_language)" title="ABC (programming language)" id="mwsw">ABC</a> programming language. Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwtA"> </span>3.0, released in 2008, was a major revision and not completely <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward-compatible" title="Backward-compatible" class="mw-redirect" id="mwtQ">backward-compatible</a> with earlier versions. Beginning with Python 3.5,<sup about="#mwt187" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-41" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-41"}}'><a href="#cite_note-41" id="mwtg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwtw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwuA">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwuQ">]</span></span></a></sup> capabilities and keywords for typing were added to the language, allowing optional <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_typing" title="Static typing" class="mw-redirect" id="mwug">static typing</a>.<sup about="#mwt190" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-42" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-42"}}'><a href="#cite_note-42" id="mwuw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwvA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwvQ">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwvg">]</span></span></a></sup> <span about="#mwt184" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwvw" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"As of","href":"./Template:As_of"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2026"}},"i":0}}]}'>As of 2026</span><sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;" about="#mwt184"><a rel="mw:ExtLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Python_(programming_language)&amp;action=edit" class="external text" data-mw-original-href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Python_(programming_language)&amp;action=edit"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span>update<span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></a></sup><span typeof="mw:Nowiki" about="#mwt184"></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements_from_2026" about="#mwt184"/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements" about="#mwt184" id="mwwA"/>, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_Software_Foundation" title="Python Software Foundation" id="mwwQ">Python Software Foundation</a> supports Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14, following the project's annual release cycle and five-year support policy. Python 3.15.0rc1 (which defaults to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8" title="UTF-8" id="mwwg">UTF-8</a>) is out in preview, and the stable release is expected to launch in October 2026.<sup about="#mwt193" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python3.15-whatsnew_43-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python3.15-whatsnew"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Python3.15-whatsnew-43"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python3.15-whatsnew-43" id="mwww"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwxA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwxQ">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwxg">]</span></span></a></sup> Earlier versions in the 3.x series have reached end-of-life and no longer receive security updates. </p>

<p id="mwxw">Python is widely taught as an introductory programming language.<sup about="#mwt196" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-44" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-44"}}'><a href="#cite_note-44" id="mwyA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwyQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwyg">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwyw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" id="mwzA" data-mw='{"autoGenerated":true}'/></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwzQ" aria-labelledby="History"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History">History</h2></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt197" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwzg" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"History of Python"}},"i":0}}]}'><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1368532237" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" about="#mwt198" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}'>.mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+.mw-empty-elt+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}</style></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt197" id="mwzw">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Python" title="History of Python">History of Python</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mw0A"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mw0Q"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg/250px-Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg/500px-Guido_van_Rossum_in_PyConUS24.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="3992" data-file-height="5976" data-file-type="bitmap" height="311" width="208" class="mw-file-element" id="mw0g"/></a><figcaption id="mw0w">The designer of Python, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_van_Rossum" title="Guido van Rossum" id="mw1A">Guido van Rossum</a>, at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PyCon" title="PyCon" class="mw-redirect" id="mw1Q">PyCon</a> US 2024</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mw1g">Python was conceived in the late 1980s<sup about="#mwt202" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-venners-interview-pt-1_13-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"venners-interview-pt-1"}}'><a href="#cite_note-venners-interview-pt-1-13" id="mw1w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw2A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw2Q">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw2g">]</span></span></a></sup> by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_van_Rossum" title="Guido van Rossum" id="mw2w">Guido van Rossum</a> at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrum_Wiskunde_&amp;_Informatica" title="Centrum Wiskunde &amp; Informatica" id="mw3A">Centrum Wiskunde &amp; Informatica</a> (CWI) in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands" title="Netherlands" id="mw3Q">Netherlands</a>.<sup about="#mwt203" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-timeline-of-python_45-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"timeline-of-python"}}'><a href="#cite_note-timeline-of-python-45" id="mw3g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw3w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw4A">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw4Q">]</span></span></a></sup> It was designed as a successor to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_(programming_language)" title="ABC (programming language)" id="mw4g">ABC</a> programming language, which was inspired by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SETL" title="SETL" id="mw4w">SETL</a>,<sup about="#mwt204" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-12_46-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-12"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-12-46" id="mw5A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw5Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw5g">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw5w">]</span></span></a></sup> capable of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exception_handling" title="Exception handling" id="mw6A">exception handling</a> and interfacing with the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amoeba_(operating_system)" title="Amoeba (operating system)" id="mw6Q">Amoeba</a> operating system.<sup about="#mwt205" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-faq-created_20-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"faq-created"}}'><a href="#cite_note-faq-created-20" id="mw6g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw6w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw7A">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw7Q">]</span></span></a></sup> Python implementation began in December<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mw7g"> </span>1989.<sup about="#mwt206" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-timeline-of-python_45-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"timeline-of-python"}}'><a href="#cite_note-timeline-of-python-45" id="mw7w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw8A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw8Q">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw8g">]</span></span></a></sup> Van Rossum first released it in 1991 as Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mw8w"> </span>0.9.0.<sup about="#mwt207" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-timeline-of-python_45-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"timeline-of-python"}}'><a href="#cite_note-timeline-of-python-45" id="mw9A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw9Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw9g">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw9w">]</span></span></a></sup> Van Rossum assumed sole responsibility for the project, as the lead developer, until 12 July 2018, when he announced his "permanent vacation" from responsibilities as Python's "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benevolent_dictator_for_life" title="Benevolent dictator for life" id="mw-A">benevolent dictator for life</a>" (BDFL); this title was bestowed on him by the Python community to reflect his long-term commitment as the project's chief decision-maker.<sup about="#mwt208" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-lj-bdfl-resignation_47-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"lj-bdfl-resignation"}}'><a href="#cite_note-lj-bdfl-resignation-47" id="mw-Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw-g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw-w">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw_A">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt199" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-48" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"lower-alpha"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-48"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"efn","href":"./Template:Efn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"He has since come out of retirement and is self-titled \"BDFL-emeritus\"&lt;!-- on his Twitter-->."}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="#cite_note-48" data-mw-group="lower-alpha" id="mw_Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw_g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw_w">[</span>c<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQA">]</span></span></a></sup> In January<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAQE"> </span>2019, active Python core developers elected a five-member Steering Council to lead the project.<sup about="#mwt211" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-49" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-49"}}'><a href="#cite_note-49" id="mwAQI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQQ">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQU">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt214" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-50" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-50"}}'><a href="#cite_note-50" id="mwAQY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQg">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAQo">The name <i id="mwAQs">Python</i> derives from the British comedy series <i id="mwAQw"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python's_Flying_Circus" title="Monty Python's Flying Circus" id="mwAQ0">Monty Python's Flying Circus</a></i>.<sup about="#mwt218" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-:0_51-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":":0"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-:0-51"}}'><a href="#cite_note-:0-51" id="mwAQ4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQ8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARA">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARE">]</span></span></a></sup> (See <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="#Naming" about="#mwt215" typeof="mw:Transclusion" class="mw-selflink-fragment" id="mwARI" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"section link","href":"./Template:Section_link"},"params":{"1":{"wt":""},"2":{"wt":"Naming"}},"i":0}}]}'>§<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>Naming</a>.)</p>

<p id="mwARM">Python 2.0 was released on 16 October 2000, featuring many new features such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_comprehension" title="List comprehension" id="mwARQ">list comprehensions</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_detection" title="Cycle detection" id="mwARU">cycle-detecting</a> garbage collection, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting" title="Reference counting" id="mwARY">reference counting</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode" title="Unicode" id="mwARc">Unicode</a> support.<sup about="#mwt219" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-newin-2.0_52-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"newin-2.0"}}'><a href="#cite_note-newin-2.0-52" id="mwARg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwARk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARo">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARs">]</span></span></a></sup> Python 2.7's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End-of-life_product" title="End-of-life product" class="mw-redirect" id="mwARw">end-of-life</a> was initially set for 2015, and then postponed to 2020 out of concern that a large body of existing code could not easily be forward-ported to Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAR0"> </span>3.<sup about="#mwt222" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-53" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-53"}}'><a href="#cite_note-53" id="mwAR4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAR8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASA">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASE">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt225" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-54" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-54"}}'><a href="#cite_note-54" id="mwASI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASQ">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASU">]</span></span></a></sup> It no longer receives security patches or updates.<sup about="#mwt228" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-55" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-55"}}'><a href="#cite_note-55" id="mwASY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASg">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASk">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt231" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-56" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-56"}}'><a href="#cite_note-56" id="mwASo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASw">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAS0">]</span></span></a></sup> While Python 2.7 and older versions are officially unsupported, a different unofficial Python implementation, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PyPy" title="PyPy" id="mwAS4">PyPy</a>, continues to support Python 2, i.e., "2.7.18+" (plus 3.11<!-- PyPy docs in Nov 2025: "Python 2.7.18 and 3.11.11", not mentioning later 3.11.14 -->), with the plus signifying (at least some) "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backported" title="Backported" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAS8">backported</a> security updates".<sup about="#mwt234" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-57" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-57"}}'><a href="#cite_note-57" id="mwATA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwATE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATI">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwATQ">Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwATU"> </span>3.0 was released on 3 December 2008, and was a major revision and not completely <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward-compatible" title="Backward-compatible" class="mw-redirect" id="mwATY">backward-compatible</a> with earlier versions, with some new semantics and changed syntax. Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwATc"> </span>2.7.18, released in 2020, was the last release of Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwATg"> </span>2.<sup about="#mwt237" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-58" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-58"}}'><a href="#cite_note-58" id="mwATk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwATo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATs">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATw">]</span></span></a></sup> Several releases in the Python 3.x series have added new syntax to the language, and made a few (considered very minor) backward-incompatible changes.</p>

<p id="mwAT0"><span about="#mwt238" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAT4" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"As of","href":"./Template:As_of"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"August 2026"}},"i":0}}]}'>As of August 2026</span><sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;" about="#mwt238"><a rel="mw:ExtLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Python_(programming_language)&amp;action=edit" class="external text" data-mw-original-href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Python_(programming_language)&amp;action=edit"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span>update<span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></a></sup><span typeof="mw:Nowiki" about="#mwt238"></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements_from_August_2026" about="#mwt238"/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements" about="#mwt238" id="mwAT8"/>, Python 3.14.7 <!-- {{wikidata|property|P548=Q2804309|P348}} --> is the latest stable release, and since 3.14 official Android binary releases are available. All older 3.x versions had a security update down to Python 3.9.24 then again with 3.9.25, the final version in 3.9 series; and then again security updates in August 2026 down to 3.10.21. Python 3.10 is, since November 2025, the oldest supported branch.<sup about="#mwt241" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-59" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-59"}}'><a href="#cite_note-59" id="mwAUA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAUE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUI">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUM">]</span></span></a></sup> Python 3.15 has release candidate 1 out. Releases receive two years of full support followed by three years of security support.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="2" id="mwAUQ" aria-labelledby="Design_philosophy_and_features"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Design_philosophy_and_features">Design philosophy and features</h2></div>
<p id="mwAUU">Python is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-paradigm_programming_language" title="Multi-paradigm programming language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAUY">multi-paradigm programming language</a>. Object-oriented programming and structured programming are fully supported, and many of their features support functional programming and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect-oriented_programming" title="Aspect-oriented programming" id="mwAUc">aspect-oriented programming</a> – including <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaprogramming" title="Metaprogramming" id="mwAUg">metaprogramming</a><sup about="#mwt243" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-13_60-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-13"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-13-60" id="mwAUk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAUo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUs">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUw">]</span></span></a></sup> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaobject" title="Metaobject" id="mwAU0">metaobjects</a>.<sup about="#mwt244" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-14_61-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-14"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-14-61" id="mwAU4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAU8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVA">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVE">]</span></span></a></sup> Many other paradigms are supported via extensions, including <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_by_contract" title="Design by contract" id="mwAVI">design by contract</a><sup about="#mwt245" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-15_62-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-15"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-15-62" id="mwAVM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAVQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVU">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt246" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-16_63-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-16"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-16-63" id="mwAVc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAVg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVk">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVo">]</span></span></a></sup> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_programming" title="Logic programming" id="mwAVs">logic programming</a>.<sup about="#mwt247" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-17_64-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-17"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-17-64" id="mwAVw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAV0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAV4">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAV8">]</span></span></a></sup> Python is often referred to as a <span style="padding-right:0.15em;" about="#mwt242" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAWA" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"italics correction","href":"./Template:Italics_correction"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"&apos;&apos;‘[[glue language]]’&apos;&apos;"}},"i":0}}]}'><i>‘<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glue_language" title="Glue language" class="mw-redirect">glue language</a>’</i></span><sup about="#mwt250" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-65" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-65"}}'><a href="#cite_note-65" id="mwAWE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAWI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWM">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWQ">]</span></span></a></sup> because it is purposely designed to be able to integrate components written in other languages.</p>

<p id="mwAWU">Python uses dynamic typing and a combination of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting" title="Reference counting" id="mwAWY">reference counting</a> and a cycle-detecting garbage collector for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_management" title="Memory management" id="mwAWc">memory management</a>.<sup about="#mwt253" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Reference_counting_66-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Reference_counting"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Reference_counting-66"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Reference_counting-66" id="mwAWg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAWk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWo">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWs">]</span></span></a></sup> It uses dynamic <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Name_resolution_(programming_languages)" title="Name resolution (programming languages)" id="mwAWw">name resolution</a> (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_binding" title="Late binding" id="mwAW0">late binding</a>), which binds method and variable names during program execution.</p>

<p id="mwAW4">Python's design offers some support for functional programming in the "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisp_(programming_language)" title="Lisp (programming language)" id="mwAW8">Lisp</a> tradition". It has <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-text mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt254" id="mwAXA" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"text","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"filter"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"filter"}},"i":0}}]}'>filter</code>, <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-text mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt256" id="mwAXE" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"text","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"map"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"map"}},"i":0}}]}'>map</code>, and <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-text mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt258" id="mwAXI" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"text","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"reduce"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"reduce"}},"i":0}}]}'>reduce</code> functions; <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_comprehension" title="List comprehension" id="mwAXM">list comprehensions</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_array" title="Associative array" id="mwAXQ">dictionaries</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)" title="Set (mathematics)" id="mwAXU">sets</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generator_(computer_programming)" title="Generator (computer programming)" id="mwAXY">generator</a> expressions.<sup about="#mwt262" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-59_67-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-59"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-59-67" id="mwAXc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAXg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXk">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXo">]</span></span></a></sup> The standard library has two modules (<code about="#mwt260" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAXs" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"codes","href":"./Template:Codes"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"itertools"}},"i":0}}]}'>itertools</code> and <code about="#mwt261" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAXw" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"codes","href":"./Template:Codes"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"functools"}},"i":0}}]}'>functools</code>) that implement functional tools borrowed from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haskell" title="Haskell" id="mwAX0">Haskell</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_ML" title="Standard ML" id="mwAX4">Standard ML</a>.<sup about="#mwt263" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-18_68-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-18"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-18-68" id="mwAX8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAYA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYE">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAYM">Python's core philosophy is summarized in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zen_of_Python" title="Zen of Python" id="mwAYQ">Zen of Python</a> (PEP 20) written by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Peters_(software_engineer)" title="Tim Peters (software engineer)" id="mwAYU">Tim Peters</a>, which includes aphorisms such as these:<sup about="#mwt264" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-PEP20_69-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"PEP20"}}'><a href="#cite_note-PEP20-69" id="mwAYY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAYc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYg">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<ul id="mwAYo"><li id="mwAYs">Explicit is better than implicit.</li>
<li id="mwAYw">Simple is better than complex.</li>
<li id="mwAY0">Readability counts.</li>
<li id="mwAY4">Special cases aren't special enough to break the rules.</li>
<li id="mwAY8">Although practicality beats purity, errors should never pass silently, unless explicitly silenced.</li>
<li id="mwAZA">There should be one—and preferably only one—obvious way to do it.</li></ul>
<!-- Note this isn't a full list, just some of the more significant aphorisms -->

<p id="mwAZE">However, Python has received criticism for violating these principles and adding unnecessary language bloat.<sup about="#mwt268" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python-Changes-2014_70-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python-Changes-2014"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Python-Changes-2014-70"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python-Changes-2014-70" id="mwAZI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZQ">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZU">]</span></span></a></sup> Responses to these criticisms note that the Zen of Python is a guideline rather than a rule.<sup about="#mwt271" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Confusion-regarding-a-rule-in-the-Zen-of-Python_71-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Confusion-regarding-a-rule-in-the-Zen-of-Python"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Confusion-regarding-a-rule-in-the-Zen-of-Python-71"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Confusion-regarding-a-rule-in-the-Zen-of-Python-71" id="mwAZY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZg">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZk">]</span></span></a></sup> The addition of some new features had been controversial: Guido van Rossum resigned as <i id="mwAZo">Benevolent Dictator for Life</i> after conflict about adding the assignment expression operator in <span class="nowrap" about="#mwt265" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAZs" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"nobr","href":"./Template:Nobr"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Python 3.8."}},"i":0}}]}'>Python 3.8.</span><sup about="#mwt274" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-The-Most-Controversial-Python-Walrus-Operator_72-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"The-Most-Controversial-Python-Walrus-Operator"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-The-Most-Controversial-Python-Walrus-Operator-72"}}'><a href="#cite_note-The-Most-Controversial-Python-Walrus-Operator-72" id="mwAZw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZ0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZ4">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZ8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt277" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-The-Controversy-Behind-The-Walrus-Operator-in-Python_73-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"The-Controversy-Behind-The-Walrus-Operator-in-Python"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-The-Controversy-Behind-The-Walrus-Operator-in-Python-73"}}'><a href="#cite_note-The-Controversy-Behind-The-Walrus-Operator-in-Python-73" id="mwAaA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAaE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaI">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAaQ">Nevertheless, rather than building all functionality into its core, Python was designed to be highly <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extensible" title="Extensible" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAaU">extensible</a> through modules. This compact modularity has made it particularly popular as a means of adding programmable interfaces to existing applications. Van Rossum's vision of a small core language with a large standard library and an easily extensible interpreter stemmed from his frustrations with ABC, which represented the opposite approach.<sup about="#mwt278" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-venners-interview-pt-1_13-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"venners-interview-pt-1"}}'><a href="#cite_note-venners-interview-pt-1-13" id="mwAaY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAac"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAag">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAak">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAao">Python claims to strive for a simpler, less-cluttered <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntax_(programming_languages)" title="Syntax (programming languages)" id="mwAas">syntax</a> and grammar, while giving developers a choice in their coding methodology. Python lacks <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_(statement)#Post-test_loop" title="Loop (statement)" id="mwAaw"><code id="mwAa0">do .. while</code> loops</a>, which <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Van_Rossum" title="Guido Van Rossum" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAa4">Rossum</a> considered harmful.<sup about="#mwt281" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-74" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-74"}}'><a href="#cite_note-74" id="mwAa8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbE">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbI">]</span></span></a></sup> In contrast to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perl" title="Perl" id="mwAbM">Perl</a>'s motto "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_is_more_than_one_way_to_do_it" title="There is more than one way to do it" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAbQ">there is more than one way to do it</a>", Python advocates an approach where "there should be one – and preferably only one – obvious way to do it".<!-- removed comment with specious demand to leave punctuation contrary to Wikipedia MOS unchanged: Reason given, to duplicate lack of spaces in quote, is a grotesquely false justification. --><sup about="#mwt282" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-PEP20_69-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"PEP20"}}'><a href="#cite_note-PEP20-69" id="mwAbU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbc">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbg">]</span></span></a></sup> In practice, however, Python provides many ways to achieve a given goal. There are at least three ways to format a string literal, with no certainty as to which one a programmer should use.<sup about="#mwt285" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python-String-Formatting-Best-Practices_75-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python-String-Formatting-Best-Practices"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Python-String-Formatting-Best-Practices-75"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python-String-Formatting-Best-Practices-75" id="mwAbk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbs">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbw">]</span></span></a></sup> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Martelli" title="Alex Martelli" id="mwAb0">Alex Martelli</a> is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow" title="Fellow" id="mwAb4">Fellow</a> at the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_Software_Foundation" title="Python Software Foundation" id="mwAb8">Python Software Foundation</a> and Python book author; he wrote that "To describe something as 'clever' is <i id="mwAcA">not</i> considered a compliment in the Python culture."<sup about="#mwt286" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-19_76-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-19"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-19-76" id="mwAcE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcM">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAcU">Python's developers typically prioritize readability over performance. For example, they reject patches to non-critical parts of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPython" title="CPython" id="mwAcY">CPython</a> reference implementation that would offer increases in speed that do not justify the cost of clarity and readability.<sup about="#mwt288" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-20_77-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-20"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-20-77" id="mwAcc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAck">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAco">]</span></span></a></sup><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_with_failed_verification" about="#mwt287" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAcs" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Failed verification","href":"./Template:Failed_verification"},"params":{"date":{"wt":"August 2025"},"reason":{"wt":"The referenced source did not mention that information. A better source should be found."}},"i":0}}]}'/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_failed_verification_from_August_2025" about="#mwt287"/><sup class="noprint Inline-Template " style="white-space:nowrap;" about="#mwt287" id="mwAcw"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span><i><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="The referenced source did not mention that information. A better source should be found. (August 2025)">failed verification</span></a></i><span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></sup> Execution speed can be improved by moving speed-critical functions to extension modules written in languages such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)" title="C (programming language)" id="mwAc0">C</a>, or by using a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just-in-time_compiler" title="Just-in-time compiler" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAc4">just-in-time compiler</a> like <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PyPy" title="PyPy" id="mwAc8">PyPy</a>. Also, it is possible to transpile to other languages. However, this approach either fails to achieve the expected speed-up, since Python is a very <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_language" title="Dynamic language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAdA">dynamic language</a>, or only a restricted subset of Python is compiled (with potential minor semantic changes).<sup about="#mwt289" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-PyJL_78-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"PyJL"}}'><a href="#cite_note-PyJL-78" id="mwAdE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdM">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAdU">Python is meant to be a fun language to use.<sup about="#mwt291" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-fun_79-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"fun"}}'><a href="#cite_note-fun-79" id="mwAdY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdg">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdk">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt290" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAdo" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"3"}},"i":0}}]}'><span title="Page / location: 3"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>3<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> This goal is reflected in the name – a tribute to the British comedy group <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python" title="Monty Python" id="mwAds">Monty Python</a><sup about="#mwt292" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-whyname_80-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"whyname"}}'><a href="#cite_note-whyname-80" id="mwAdw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAd0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAd4">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAd8">]</span></span></a></sup> – and in playful approaches to some tutorials and reference materials. For instance, some code examples use the terms "spam" and "eggs" (in reference to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spam_(Monty_Python)" title="Spam (Monty Python)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAeA">a Monty Python sketch</a>), rather than the typical terms <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foobar" title="Foobar" id="mwAeE">"foo" and "bar"</a>.<sup about="#mwt295" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-fun_79-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"fun"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-fun-79"}}'><a href="#cite_note-fun-79" id="mwAeI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAeM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeQ">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeU">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt298" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pprint-doc_81-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pprint-doc"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-pprint-doc-81"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pprint-doc-81" id="mwAeY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAec"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeg">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAek">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAeo">A common <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neologism" title="Neologism" id="mwAes">neologism</a> in the Python community is <i id="mwAew">pythonic</i>, which has a broad range of meanings related to program style: Pythonic code may use Python <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_idiom" title="Programming idiom" id="mwAe0">idioms</a> well; be natural or show fluency in the language; or conform with Python's minimalist philosophy and emphasis on readability.<sup about="#mwt301" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-82" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-82"}}'><a href="#cite_note-82" id="mwAe4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAe8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfA">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfE">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<section data-mw-section-id="3" id="mwAfI" aria-labelledby="Enhancement_Proposals"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Enhancement_Proposals">Enhancement Proposals</h3></div>
