typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt344">–</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt344"> </span>257 and others.<sup about="#mwt345" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-believemy_89-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"believemy","group":""},"body":{"html":""},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"refn","href":"./Template:Refn"},"params":{"name":{"wt":"\"believemy\""}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="#cite_note-believemy-89" id="mwAig"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAik"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAio">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAis">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="4" id="mwAiw" aria-labelledby="Syntax_and_semantics"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Syntax_and_semantics">Syntax and semantics</h2></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt349" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAi0" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Python syntax and semantics"}},"i":0}}]}'><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237" about="#mwt350" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}'/></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt349" id="mwAi4">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_syntax_and_semantics" title="Python syntax and semantics">Python syntax and semantics</a></div>

<p id="mwAi8">Python is meant to be an easily readable language. Its formatting is visually uncluttered and often uses English keywords where other languages use punctuation. Unlike many other languages, it does not use <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curly_bracket_programming_language" title="Curly bracket programming language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAjA">curly brackets</a> to delimit blocks, and semicolons after statements are allowed but rarely used. It has fewer syntactic exceptions and special cases than <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)" title="C (programming language)" id="mwAjE">C</a> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(programming_language)" title="Pascal (programming language)" id="mwAjI">Pascal</a>.<sup about="#mwt351" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-52_90-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-52"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-52-90" id="mwAjM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAjQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjU">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<section data-mw-section-id="5" id="mwAjc" aria-labelledby="Indentation"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Indentation">Indentation</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt352" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAjg" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Further","href":"./Template:Further"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Python syntax and semantics#Indentation"}},"i":0}}]}'><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237" about="#mwt353" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}'/></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt352" id="mwAjk">Further information: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_syntax_and_semantics#Indentation" title="Python syntax and semantics">Python syntax and semantics §<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>Indentation</a></div>

<p id="mwAjo">Python uses <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitespace_character" title="Whitespace character" id="mwAjs">whitespace</a> indentation, rather than curly brackets or keywords, to delimit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_(programming)" title="Block (programming)" id="mwAjw">blocks</a>. An increase in indentation comes after certain statements; a decrease in indentation signifies the end of the current block.<sup about="#mwt354" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-53_91-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-53"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-53-91" id="mwAj0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAj4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAj8">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkA">]</span></span></a></sup> Thus, the program's visual structure accurately represents its semantic structure.<sup about="#mwt357" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-guttag_92-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"guttag"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-guttag-92"}}'><a href="#cite_note-guttag-92" id="mwAkE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkM">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkQ">]</span></span></a></sup> This feature is sometimes termed the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-side_rule" title="Off-side rule" id="mwAkU">off-side rule</a>. Some other languages use indentation this way; but in most, indentation has no semantic meaning. The recommended indent size is four spaces.<sup about="#mwt360" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pep8_93-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pep8"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-pep8-93"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pep8-93" id="mwAkY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkg">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mwAko" aria-labelledby="Statements_and_control_flow"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Statements_and_control_flow">Statements and control flow</h3></div>
<p id="mwAks">Python's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statement_(computer_science)" title="Statement (computer science)" id="mwAkw">statements</a> include the following:</p>
<ul id="mwAk0"><li id="mwAk4">The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assignment_(computer_science)" title="Assignment (computer science)" id="mwAk8">assignment</a> statement, using a single equals sign <code id="mwAlA">=</code></li>
<li id="mwAlE">The <code id="mwAlI"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If-then-else" title="If-then-else" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAlM">if</a></code> statement, which conditionally executes a block of code, along with <code id="mwAlQ"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_(computer_programming)#If–then(–else)" title="Conditional (computer programming)" id="mwAlU">else</a></code> and <code id="mwAlY">elif</code> (a contraction of <code id="mwAlc"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_(computer_programming)#Else_if" title="Conditional (computer programming)" id="mwAlg">else if</a></code>)</li>
<li id="mwAlk">The <code id="mwAlo"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreach#Python" title="Foreach" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAls">for</a></code> statement, which iterates over an <i id="mwAlw">iterable</i> object, capturing each element to a variable for use by the attached block; the variable is not deleted when the loop finishes</li>
<li id="mwAl0">The <code id="mwAl4"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/While_loop#Python" title="While loop" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAl8">while</a></code> statement, which executes a block of code as long as boolean condition is true</li>
<li id="mwAmA">The <code id="mwAmE"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exception_handling_syntax#Python" title="Exception handling syntax" id="mwAmI">try</a></code> statement, which allows exceptions raised in its attached code block to be caught and handled by <code id="mwAmM">except</code> clauses (or new syntax <code id="mwAmQ">except*</code> in Python 3.11 for exception groups);<sup about="#mwt363" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-94" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-94"}}'><a href="#cite_note-94" id="mwAmU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmc">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmg">]</span></span></a></sup> the <code id="mwAmk">try</code> statement also ensures that clean-up code in a <code id="mwAmo">finally</code> block is always run regardless of how the block exits</li>
<li id="mwAms">The <code id="mwAmw">raise</code> statement, used to raise a specified exception or re-raise a caught exception</li>
<li id="mwAm0">The <code id="mwAm4">class</code> statement, which executes a block of code and attaches its local namespace to a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_(computer_science)" title="Class (computer science)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAm8">class</a>, for use in object-oriented programming</li>
<li id="mwAnA">The <code id="mwAnE">def</code> statement, which defines a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(computer_programming)" title="Function (computer programming)" id="mwAnI">function</a> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_(computing)" title="Method (computing)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAnM">method</a></li>
<li id="mwAnQ">The <code id="mwAnU"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dispose_pattern#Language_constructs" title="Dispose pattern" id="mwAnY">with</a></code> statement, which encloses a code block within a context manager, allowing <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization" title="Resource acquisition is initialization" id="mwAnc">resource-acquisition-is-initialization</a> (RAII)-like behavior and replacing a common try/finally idiom<sup about="#mwt366" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-95" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-95"}}'><a href="#cite_note-95" id="mwAng"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAnk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAno">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAns">]</span></span></a></sup> Examples of a context include acquiring a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lock_(computer_science)" title="Lock (computer science)" id="mwAnw">lock</a> before some code is run, and then releasing the lock; or opening and then closing a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_file" title="Computer file" id="mwAn0">file</a></li>
<li id="mwAn4">The <code id="mwAn8"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break_statement" title="Break statement" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAoA">break</a></code> statement, which exits a loop</li>
<li id="mwAoE">The <code id="mwAoI">continue</code> statement, which skips the rest of the current iteration and continues with the next</li>
<li id="mwAoM">The <code id="mwAoQ">del</code> statement, which removes a variable—deleting the reference from the name to the value, and producing an error if the variable is referred to before it is redefined<sup about="#mwt367" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-96" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"lower-alpha"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-96"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"efn","href":"./Template:Efn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"&lt;code>del&lt;/code> in Python does not behave the same way &lt;code>delete&lt;/code> in languages such as [[C++]] does, where such a word is used to call the [[Destructor (computer programming)|destructor]] and deallocate heap memory."}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="#cite_note-96" data-mw-group="lower-alpha" id="mwAoU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAoY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoc">[</span>d<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAog">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwAok">The <code id="mwAoo">pass</code> statement, serving as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOP_(code)" title="NOP (code)" id="mwAos">NOP</a> (i.e., no operation), which is syntactically needed to create an empty code block</li>
<li id="mwAow">The <code id="mwAo0"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assertion_(programming)" title="Assertion (programming)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAo4">assert</a></code> statement, used in debugging to check for conditions that should apply</li>
<li id="mwAo8">The <code id="mwApA">yield</code> statement, which returns a value from a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generator_(computer_programming)#Python" title="Generator (computer programming)" id="mwApE">generator</a> function (and also an operator); used to implement <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coroutine" title="Coroutine" id="mwApI">coroutines</a></li>
<li id="mwApM">The <code id="mwApQ">return</code> statement, used to return a value from a function</li>
<li id="mwApU">The <code id="mwApY"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Include_directive" title="Include directive" id="mwApc">import</a></code> and <code id="mwApg">from</code> statements, used to import modules whose functions or variables can be used in the current program. Python 3.15 adds a new functionality to lazily import with a new keyword: "The <code id="mwApk">lazy</code> keyword works with both <code id="mwApo">import</code> and <code id="mwAps">from ... import</code> statements."<sup about="#mwt370" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python3.15-whatsnew_43-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python3.15-whatsnew"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python3.15-whatsnew-43" id="mwApw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAp0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAp4">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAp8">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwAqA">The <code id="mwAqE">match</code> and <code id="mwAqI">case</code> statements, analogous to a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switch_statement" title="Switch statement" id="mwAqM">switch statement</a> construct, which compares an expression against one or more cases as a control-flow measure</li></ul>

<p id="mwAqQ">The assignment statement (<code id="mwAqU">=</code>) binds a name as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointer_(computer_programming)" title="Pointer (computer programming)" id="mwAqY">reference</a> to a separate, dynamically allocated <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_(computer_science)" title="Object (computer science)" id="mwAqc">object</a>. Variables may subsequently be rebound at any time to any object. In Python, a variable name is a generic reference holder without a fixed <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_system" title="Type system" id="mwAqg">data type</a>; however, it always refers to <i id="mwAqk">some</i> object with a type. This is called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_system#Dynamic_type_checking_and_runtime_type_information" title="Type system" id="mwAqo">dynamic typing</a>—in contrast to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statically-typed" title="Statically-typed" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAqs">statically-typed</a> languages, where each variable may contain only a value of a certain type.</p>

<p id="mwAqw">Python does not support <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tail_call" title="Tail call" id="mwAq0">tail call</a> optimization or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-class_continuations" title="First-class continuations" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAq4">first-class continuations</a>; according to Van Rossum, the language never will.<sup about="#mwt371" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-55_97-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-55"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-55-97" id="mwAq8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwArA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArE">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArI">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt372" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-56_98-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-56"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-56-98" id="mwArM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwArQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArU">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArY">]</span></span></a></sup> However, better support for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coroutine" title="Coroutine" id="mwArc">coroutine</a>-like functionality is provided by extending Python's generators.<sup about="#mwt373" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-57_99-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-57"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-57-99" id="mwArg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwArk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAro">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArs">]</span></span></a></sup> Before 2.5, generators were <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_evaluation" title="Lazy evaluation" id="mwArw">lazy</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterator" title="Iterator" id="mwAr0">iterators</a>; data was passed unidirectionally out of the generator. From Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAr4"> </span>2.5 on, it is possible to pass data back into a generator function; and from version 3.3, data can be passed through multiple stack levels.<sup about="#mwt374" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-58_100-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-58"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-58-100" id="mwAr8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAsA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAsE">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAsI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="7" id="mwAsM" aria-labelledby="Expressions"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Expressions">Expressions</h3></div>
<p id="mwAsQ">Python's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_(computer_science)" title="Expression (computer science)" id="mwAsU">expressions</a> include the following:</p>
<ul id="mwAsY"><li id="mwAsc">The <code id="mwAsg">+</code>, <code id="mwAsk">-</code>, and <code id="mwAso">*</code> operators for mathematical addition, subtraction, and multiplication are similar to other languages, but the behavior of division differs. There are two types of division in Python: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_division" title="Floor division" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAss">floor division</a> (or integer division) <code id="mwAsw">//</code>, and floating-point division <code id="mwAs0">/</code>.<sup about="#mwt377" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-101" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-101"}}'><a href="#cite_note-101" id="mwAs4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAs8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAtA">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAtE">]</span></span></a></sup> Python uses the <code id="mwAtI">**</code> operator for exponentiation.</li>
<li id="mwAtM">Python uses the <code id="mwAtQ">+</code> operator for string concatenation. The language uses the <code id="mwAtU">*</code> operator for duplicating a string a specified number of times.</li>
<li id="mwAtY">The <code id="mwAtc">@</code> infix operator<!-- was introduced in Python 3.5--> is intended to be used by libraries such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NumPy" title="NumPy" id="mwAtg">NumPy</a> for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_multiplication" title="Matrix multiplication" id="mwAtk">matrix multiplication</a>.<sup about="#mwt380" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-PEP465_102-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"PEP465"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-PEP465-102"}}'><a href="#cite_note-PEP465-102" id="mwAto"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAts"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAtw">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAt0">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt383" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python3.5Changelog_103-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python3.5Changelog"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Python3.5Changelog-103"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python3.5Changelog-103" id="mwAt4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAt8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuA">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuE">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwAuI">The syntax <code id="mwAuM">:=</code>, called the "<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1349394836" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt384" id="mwAuQ" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Template:Visible anchor/styles.css"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"va","href":"./Template:Va"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"walrus operator"}},"i":0}}]}'>.mw-parser-output .vanchor>:target~.vanchor-text{background-color:#ebf4ff}@media screen{html.skin-theme-clientpref-night .mw-parser-output .vanchor>:target~.vanchor-text{background-color:#0f4dc9}}@media screen and (prefers-color-scheme:dark){html.skin-theme-clientpref-os .mw-parser-output .vanchor>:target~.vanchor-text{background-color:#0f4dc9}}</style><span class="vanchor" about="#mwt384" id="mwAuU"><span id="walrus_operator"></span><span class="vanchor-text">walrus operator</span></span>", was introduced in Python 3.8. This operator assigns values to variables as part of a larger expression.<sup about="#mwt388" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Python3.8Changelog_104-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Python3.8Changelog"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Python3.8Changelog-104"}}'><a href="#cite_note-Python3.8Changelog-104" id="mwAuY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAuc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAug">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuk">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwAuo">In Python, <code id="mwAus">==</code> compares two objects by value. Python's <code id="mwAuw">is</code> operator may be used to compare object identities (i.e., comparison by reference), and comparisons may be chained—for example, <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt389" id="mwAu0" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"a &lt;= b &lt;= c"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"a &lt;= b &lt;= c"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwAu4">a</span> <span class="o" id="mwAu8">&lt;=</span> <span class="n" id="mwAvA">b</span> <span class="o" id="mwAvE">&lt;=</span> <span class="n" id="mwAvI">c</span></code>.</li>
<li id="mwAvM">Python uses <code id="mwAvQ">and</code>, <code id="mwAvU">or</code>, and <code id="mwAvY">not</code> as Boolean operators.</li>
<li id="mwAvc">Python has a type of expression called a <i id="mwAvg"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_comprehension#Python" title="List comprehension" id="mwAvk">list comprehension</a></i>, and a more general expression called a <i id="mwAvo">generator expression</i>.<sup about="#mwt391" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-59_67-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-59"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-59-67" id="mwAvs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv0">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv4">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwAv8"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_function" title="Anonymous function" id="mwAwA">Anonymous functions</a> are implemented using <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_(programming)" title="Lambda (programming)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAwE">lambda expressions</a>; however, there may be only one expression in each body.</li>
<li id="mwAwI">Conditional expressions are written as <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt392" id="mwAwM" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"x if c else y"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"x if c else y"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwAwQ">x</span> <span class="k" id="mwAwU">if</span> <span class="n" id="mwAwY">c</span> <span class="k" id="mwAwc">else</span> <span class="n" id="mwAwg">y</span></code>.<sup about="#mwt394" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-60_105-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-60"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-60-105" id="mwAwk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAws">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAww">]</span></span></a></sup> (This is different in operand order from the <code id="mwAw0"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%3F:" title="?:" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAw4">c<span typeof="mw:DisplaySpace" id="mwAw8"> </span>? x<span typeof="mw:DisplaySpace" id="mwAxA"> </span>: y</a></code> operator common to many other languages.)</li>
<li id="mwAxE">Python makes a distinction between <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_(computer_science)" title="List (computer science)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAxI">lists</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuple" title="Tuple" id="mwAxM">tuples</a>. Lists are written as <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt395" id="mwAxQ" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"[1, 2, 3]"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"[1, 2, 3]"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="p" id="mwAxU">[</span><span class="mi" id="mwAxY">1</span><span class="p" id="mwAxc">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAxg">2</span><span class="p" id="mwAxk">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAxo">3</span><span class="p" id="mwAxs">]</span></code>, are mutable, and cannot be used as the keys of dictionaries (since dictionary keys must be <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable" title="Immutable" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAxw">immutable</a> in Python). Tuples, written as <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt397" id="mwAx0" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"(1, 2, 3)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"(1, 2, 3)"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="p" id="mwAx4">(</span><span class="mi" id="mwAx8">1</span><span class="p" id="mwAyA">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAyE">2</span><span class="p" id="mwAyI">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAyM">3</span><span class="p" id="mwAyQ">)</span></code>, are immutable and thus can be used as the keys of dictionaries, provided that all of the tuple's elements are immutable. The <code id="mwAyU">+</code> operator can be used to concatenate two tuples, which does not directly modify their contents, but produces a new tuple containing the elements of both. For example, given the variable <code id="mwAyY">t</code> initially equal to <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt399" id="mwAyc" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"(1, 2, 3)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"(1, 2, 3)"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="p" id="mwAyg">(</span><span class="mi" id="mwAyk">1</span><span class="p" id="mwAyo">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAys">2</span><span class="p" id="mwAyw">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAy0">3</span><span class="p" id="mwAy4">)</span></code>, executing <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt401" id="mwAy8" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"t = t + (4, 5)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"t = t + (4, 5)"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwAzA">t</span> <span class="o" id="mwAzE">=</span> <span class="n" id="mwAzI">t</span> <span class="o" id="mwAzM">+</span> <span class="p" id="mwAzQ">(</span><span class="mi" id="mwAzU">4</span><span class="p" id="mwAzY">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAzc">5</span><span class="p" id="mwAzg">)</span></code> first evaluates <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt403" id="mwAzk" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"t + (4, 5)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"t + (4, 5)"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwAzo">t</span> <span class="o" id="mwAzs">+</span> <span class="p" id="mwAzw">(</span><span class="mi" id="mwAz0">4</span><span class="p" id="mwAz4">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwAz8">5</span><span class="p" id="mwA0A">)</span></code>, which yields <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt405" id="mwA0E" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="p" id="mwA0I">(</span><span class="mi" id="mwA0M">1</span><span class="p" id="mwA0Q">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA0U">2</span><span class="p" id="mwA0Y">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA0c">3</span><span class="p" id="mwA0g">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA0k">4</span><span class="p" id="mwA0o">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA0s">5</span><span class="p" id="mwA0w">)</span></code>; this result is then assigned back to <code id="mwA00">t</code>—thereby effectively "modifying the contents" of <code id="mwA04">t</code> while conforming to the immutable nature of tuple objects. Parentheses are optional for tuples in unambiguous contexts.<sup about="#mwt409" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-106" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-106"}}'><a href="#cite_note-106" id="mwA08"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1E">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1I">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwA1M">Python features <i id="mwA1Q">sequence unpacking</i> where multiple expressions, each evaluating to something assignable (e.g., a variable or a writable property) are associated just as in forming tuple literal; as a whole, the results are then put on the left-hand side of the equal sign in an assignment statement. This statement expects an <i id="mwA1U">iterable</i> object on the right-hand side of the equal sign to produce the same number of values as the writable expressions on the left-hand side; while iterating, the statement assigns each of the values produced on the right to the corresponding expression on the left.<sup about="#mwt412" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-107" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-107"}}'><a href="#cite_note-107" id="mwA1Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1g">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1k">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwA1o">Python has a "string format" operator <code id="mwA1s">%</code> that functions analogously to <code id="mwA1w"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printf" title="Printf" id="mwA10">printf</a></code> format strings in the C language—e.g. <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt413" id="mwA14" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"\"spam=%s eggs=%d\" % (\"blah\", 2)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"\"spam=%s eggs=%d\" % (\"blah\", 2)"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="s2" id="mwA18">"spam=</span><span class="si" id="mwA2A">%s</span><span class="s2" id="mwA2E"> eggs=</span><span class="si" id="mwA2I">%d</span><span class="s2" id="mwA2M">"</span> <span class="o" id="mwA2Q">%</span> <span class="p" id="mwA2U">(</span><span class="s2" id="mwA2Y">"blah"</span><span class="p" id="mwA2c">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA2g">2</span><span class="p" id="mwA2k">)</span></code> evaluates to <code id="mwA2o">"spam=blah eggs=2"</code>. In Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwA2s"> </span>2.6+ and 3+, this operator was supplemented by the <code id="mwA2w">format()</code> method of the <code id="mwA20">str</code> class, e.g., <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt415" id="mwA24" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"\"spam={0} eggs={1}\".format(\"blah\", 2)"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"\"spam={0} eggs={1}\".format(\"blah\", 2)"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="s2" id="mwA28">"spam=</span><span class="si" id="mwA3A">{0}</span><span class="s2" id="mwA3E"> eggs=</span><span class="si" id="mwA3I">{1}</span><span class="s2" id="mwA3M">"</span><span class="o" id="mwA3Q">.</span><span class="n" id="mwA3U">format</span><span class="p" id="mwA3Y">(</span><span class="s2" id="mwA3c">"blah"</span><span class="p" id="mwA3g">,</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA3k">2</span><span class="p" id="mwA3o">)</span></code>. Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwA3s"> </span>3.6 added "f-strings": <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt417" id="mwA3w" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"spam = \"blah\"; eggs = 2; f&apos;spam={spam} eggs={eggs}&apos;"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"spam = \"blah\"; eggs = 2; f&apos;spam={spam} eggs={eggs}&apos;"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA30">spam</span> <span class="o" id="mwA34">=</span> <span class="s2" id="mwA38">"blah"</span><span class="p" id="mwA4A">;</span> <span class="n" id="mwA4E">eggs</span> <span class="o" id="mwA4I">=</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA4M">2</span><span class="p" id="mwA4Q">;</span> <span class="sa" id="mwA4U">f</span><span class="s1" id="mwA4Y">'spam=</span><span class="si" id="mwA4c">{</span><span class="n" id="mwA4g">spam</span><span class="si" id="mwA4k">}</span><span class="s1" id="mwA4o"> eggs=</span><span class="si" id="mwA4s">{</span><span class="n" id="mwA4w">eggs</span><span class="si" id="mwA40">}</span><span class="s1" id="mwA44">'</span></code>.<sup about="#mwt421" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pep-0498_108-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pep-0498"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-pep-0498-108"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pep-0498-108" id="mwA48"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA5A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5E">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5I">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwA5M">Strings in Python can be <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concatenated" title="Concatenated" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA5Q">concatenated</a> by "adding" them (using the same operator as for adding integers and floats); e.g., <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt422" id="mwA5U" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"\"spam\" + \"eggs\""},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"\"spam\" + \"eggs\""},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="s2" id="mwA5Y">"spam"</span> <span class="o" id="mwA5c">+</span> <span class="s2" id="mwA5g">"eggs"</span></code> returns <code id="mwA5k">"spameggs"</code>. If strings contain numbers, they are concatenated as strings rather than as integers, e.g. <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt424" id="mwA5o" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"\"2\" + \"2\""},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"\"2\" + \"2\""},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="s2" id="mwA5s">"2"</span> <span class="o" id="mwA5w">+</span> <span class="s2" id="mwA50">"2"</span></code> returns <code id="mwA54">"22"</code>.</li>
<li id="mwA58">Python supports <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_literal" title="String literal" id="mwA6A">string literals</a> in several ways:
<ul id="mwA6E"><li id="mwA6I">Delimited by single or double quotation marks; single and double quotation marks have equivalent functionality (unlike in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_shell" title="Unix shell" id="mwA6M">Unix shells</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perl" title="Perl" id="mwA6Q">Perl</a>, and Perl-influenced languages). Both marks use the backslash (<code id="mwA6U">\</code>) as an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_character" title="Escape character" id="mwA6Y">escape character</a>. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_interpolation" title="String interpolation" id="mwA6c">String interpolation</a> became available in Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwA6g"> </span>3.6 as "formatted string literals".<sup about="#mwt426" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pep-0498_108-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pep-0498"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pep-0498-108" id="mwA6k"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA6o"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6s">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6w">]</span></span></a></sup></li>
<li id="mwA60">Triple-quoted, i.e., starting and ending with three single or double quotation marks; this may span multiple lines and function like <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here_document" title="Here document" id="mwA64">here documents</a> in shells, Perl, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_(programming_language)" title="Ruby (programming language)" id="mwA68">Ruby</a>.</li>
<li id="mwA7A"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raw_string" title="Raw string" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA7E">Raw string</a> varieties, denoted by prefixing the string literal with <code id="mwA7I">r</code>. Escape sequences are not interpreted; hence raw strings are useful where literal backslashes are common, such as in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression" title="Regular expression" id="mwA7M">regular expressions</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows" title="Windows" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA7Q">Windows</a>-style paths. (Compare "<code id="mwA7U">@</code>-quoting" in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Sharp_(programming_language)" title="C Sharp (programming language)" id="mwA7Y">C#</a>.)</li></ul></li>
<li id="mwA7c">Python has <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_index" title="Array index" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA7g">array index</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_slicing" title="Array slicing" id="mwA7k">array slicing</a> expressions in lists, which are written as <code id="mwA7o">a[key]</code>, <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt427" id="mwA7s" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"a[start:stop]"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"a[start:stop]"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA7w">a</span><span class="p" id="mwA70">[</span><span class="n" id="mwA74">start</span><span class="p" id="mwA78">:</span><span class="n" id="mwA8A">stop</span><span class="p" id="mwA8E">]</span></code> or <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt429" id="mwA8I" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"a[start:stop:step]"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"a[start:stop:step]"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA8M">a</span><span class="p" id="mwA8Q">[</span><span class="n" id="mwA8U">start</span><span class="p" id="mwA8Y">:</span><span class="n" id="mwA8c">stop</span><span class="p" id="mwA8g">:</span><span class="n" id="mwA8k">step</span><span class="p" id="mwA8o">]</span></code>. Indexes are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-based" title="Zero-based" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA8s">zero-based</a>, and negative indexes are relative to the end. Slices take elements from the <i id="mwA8w">start</i> index up to, but not including, the <i id="mwA80">stop</i> index. The (optional) third slice <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter_(computer_programming)" title="Parameter (computer programming)" id="mwA84">parameter</a>, called <i id="mwA88">step</i> or <i id="mwA9A">stride</i>, allows elements to be skipped or reversed. Slice indexes may be omitted—for example, <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt431" id="mwA9E" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"a[:]"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"a[:]"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA9I">a</span><span class="p" id="mwA9M">[:]</span></code> returns a copy of the entire list. Each element of a slice is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shallow_copy" title="Shallow copy" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA9Q">shallow copy</a>.</li></ul>

<p id="mwA9U">In Python, a distinction between expressions and statements is rigidly enforced, in contrast to languages such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Lisp" title="Common Lisp" id="mwA9Y">Common Lisp</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(programming_language)" title="Scheme (programming language)" id="mwA9c">Scheme</a>, or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_(programming_language)" title="Ruby (programming language)" id="mwA9g">Ruby</a>. This distinction leads to duplicating some functionality, for example:</p>
<ul id="mwA9k"><li id="mwA9o"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_comprehensions" title="List comprehensions" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA9s">List comprehensions</a> vs. <code id="mwA9w">for</code>-loops</li>
<li id="mwA90"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_(computer_programming)" title="Conditional (computer programming)" id="mwA94">Conditional</a> expressions vs. <code id="mwA98">if</code> blocks</li>
<li id="mwA-A">The <code id="mwA-E">eval()</code> vs. <code id="mwA-I">exec()</code> built-in functions (in Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwA-M"> </span>2, <code id="mwA-Q">exec</code> is a statement); the former function is for expressions, while the latter is for statements</li></ul>

<p id="mwA-U">A statement cannot be part of an expression; because of this restriction, expressions such as list and <code id="mwA-Y">dict</code> comprehensions (and lambda expressions) cannot contain statements. As a particular case, an assignment statement such as <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt433" id="mwA-c" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"a = 1"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"a = 1"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA-g">a</span> <span class="o" id="mwA-k">=</span> <span class="mi" id="mwA-o">1</span></code> cannot be part of the conditional expression of a conditional statement.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="8" id="mwA-s" aria-labelledby="Typing"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Typing">Typing</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwA-w"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwA-0"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg/250px-Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg/500px-Python_3.13_Standrd_Type_Hierarchy-en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="566" data-file-height="566" data-file-type="drawing" height="250" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwA-4"/></a><figcaption id="mwA-8">The standard type hierarchy in Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwA_A"> </span>3</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwA_E">Python uses <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_typing" title="Duck typing" id="mwA_I">duck typing</a>, and it has typed objects but untyped variable names. Type constraints are not checked at definition time; rather, operations on an object may fail at usage time, indicating that the object is not of an appropriate type. Despite being <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamically_typed" title="Dynamically typed" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_M">dynamically typed</a>, Python is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strongly_typed" title="Strongly typed" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_Q">strongly typed</a>, forbidding operations that are poorly defined (e.g., adding a number and a string) rather than quietly attempting to interpret them.</p>

<p id="mwA_U">Python allows programmers to define their own types using <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_(computer_science)" title="Class (computer science)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_Y">classes</a>, most often for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming" title="Object-oriented programming" id="mwA_c">object-oriented programming</a>. New <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_(computer_science)" title="Object (computer science)" id="mwA_g">instances</a> of classes are constructed by calling the class, for example, <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt435" id="mwA_k" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"SpamClass()"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"SpamClass()"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA_o">SpamClass</span><span class="p" id="mwA_s">()</span></code> or <code class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt437" id="mwA_w" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"EggsClass()"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"lang":{"wt":"python"},"code":{"wt":"EggsClass()"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwA_0">EggsClass</span><span class="p" id="mwA_4">()</span></code>); the classes are instances of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaclass" title="Metaclass" id="mwA_8">metaclass</a> <code id="mwBAA">type</code> (which is an instance of itself), thereby allowing metaprogramming and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflective_programming" title="Reflective programming" id="mwBAE">reflection</a>.</p>

<p id="mwBAI">Before version 3.0, Python had two kinds of classes, both using the same syntax: <i id="mwBAM">old-style</i> and <i id="mwBAQ">new-style</i>.<sup about="#mwt439" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-classy_109-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"classy"}}'><a href="#cite_note-classy-109" id="mwBAU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBAY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAc">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAg">]</span></span></a></sup> Current Python versions support the semantics of only the new style.</p>

<p id="mwBAk">Python supports <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optional_typing" title="Optional typing" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBAo">optional type annotations</a>.<sup about="#mwt442" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-type_hint-PEP_5-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"type_hint-PEP"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-type_hint-PEP-5"}}'><a href="#cite_note-type_hint-PEP-5" id="mwBAs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBAw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBA0">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBA4">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt445" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-110" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-110"}}'><a href="#cite_note-110" id="mwBA8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBE">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBI">]</span></span></a></sup> These annotations are not enforced by the language, but may be used by external tools such as <b id="mwBBM">mypy</b> to catch errors. Python includes a module <code id="mwBBQ">typing</code> including several type names for type annotations.<sup about="#mwt448" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-111" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-111"}}'><a href="#cite_note-111" id="mwBBU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBc">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt451" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-112" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-112"}}'><a href="#cite_note-112" id="mwBBk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBs">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBw">]</span></span></a></sup> Also, mypy supports a Python compiler called mypyc, which leverages type annotations for optimization.<sup about="#mwt454" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-113" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-113"}}'><a href="#cite_note-113" id="mwBB0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBB4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBB8">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<tr id="mwBKY">
<td id="mwBKc"><code id="mwBKg">float</code></td>
<td id="mwBKk">immutable</td>
<td id="mwBKo">64-bit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-precision" title="Double-precision" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBKs">double-precision</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_number" title="Floating-point number" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBKw">floating-point number</a> (<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754" title="IEEE 754" id="mwBK0">IEEE 754</a> number with 53<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwBK4"> </span>bits of precision, in all supported versions since CPython 3.11;<sup about="#mwt487" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-114" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-114"}}'><a href="#cite_note-114" id="mwBK8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBLA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLE">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLI">]</span></span></a></sup> <small id="mwBLM">also in practice in 3.10 and older<!-- except on e.g. VAX -->, though technically there the precision is machine-dependent<sup about="#mwt490" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-115" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-115"}}'><a href="#cite_note-115" id="mwBLQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBLU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLY">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLc">]</span></span></a></sup>)</small>.  Python's built-in type <code id="mwBLg">memoryview</code> does though support both 64-bit doubles and 32-bit floats, and Python's standard library <code id="mwBLk">struct</code> module additionally supports 16-bit half-floats. Python packages like NumPy and Pandas may also support 32-bit floats or more, e.g. <code id="mwBLo">numpy.half</code>; though support for half-floats is often incomplete or non-existent in most packages.<sup about="#mwt493" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-116" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-116"}}'><a href="#cite_note-116" id="mwBLs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBLw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBL0">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBL4">]</span></span></a></sup> <small id="mwBL8">16-bit <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bfloat16_floating-point_format" title="Bfloat16 floating-point format" id="mwBMA">bfloat</a> has support in a few packages.<sup about="#mwt496" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-117" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-117"}}'><a href="#cite_note-117" id="mwBME"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBMI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMM">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMQ">]</span></span></a></sup></small>

<p id="mwBMU"><small id="mwBMY">Most Python implementations choose to support the double kind, but some unusual (subset) implementations, such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroPython" title="MicroPython" id="mwBMc">MicroPython</a> for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedded_programming" title="Embedded programming" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBMg">embedded programming</a>, support 32-bit IEEE floats as their default float. Users can opt into 64-bit by setting MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL to MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_DOUBLE.</small></p></td>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="9" id="mwBXA" aria-labelledby="Arithmetic_operations"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Arithmetic_operations">Arithmetic operations</h3></div>
<p id="mwBXE">Python includes conventional symbols for arithmetic operators (<code id="mwBXI">+</code>, <code id="mwBXM">-</code>, <code id="mwBXQ">*</code>, <code id="mwBXU">/</code>), the floor-division operator <code id="mwBXY">//</code>, and the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo_operator" title="Modulo operator" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBXc">modulo operator</a> <code id="mwBXg">%</code>. (With the modulo operator, a remainder can be negative,<!--unlike in C language depending on compiler,<ref&#x3E;{{Cite web|url=https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11720656/modulo&#x2D;operation&#x2D;with&#x2D;negative&#x2D;numbers/42131603|title=c – Modulo operation with negative numbers|quote=Note that, in C89, whether the result round upward or downward is implementation&#x2D;defined.|website=Stack Overflow|access&#x2D;date=25 September 2019}}</ref&#x3E;--> e.g., <code id="mwBXk">4<span typeof="mw:DisplaySpace" id="mwBXo"> </span>% -3 == -2</code>.) Python also offers the <code id="mwBXs">**</code> symbol for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation" title="Exponentiation" id="mwBXw">exponentiation</a>, e.g. <code id="mwBX0">5**3 == 125</code> and <code id="mwBX4">9**0.5 == 3.0</code>, as well as the matrix‑multiplication operator <code id="mwBX8">@</code>.<sup about="#mwt538" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-120" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-120"}}'><a href="#cite_note-120" id="mwBYA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBYE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYI">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYM">]</span></span></a></sup> These operators work as in traditional mathematics; with the same <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_operations" title="Order of operations" id="mwBYQ">precedence rules</a>, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infix_notation" title="Infix notation" id="mwBYU">infix</a> operators <code id="mwBYY">+</code> and <code id="mwBYc">-</code> can also be <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unary_operation" title="Unary operation" id="mwBYg">unary</a>, to represent positive and negative numbers respectively.</p>

<p id="mwBYk">Division between integers produces floating-point results. The behavior of division has changed significantly over time:<sup about="#mwt539" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pep0238_121-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pep0238"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pep0238-121" id="mwBYo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBYs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYw">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBY0">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<ul id="mwBY4"><li id="mwBY8">The current version of Python (i.e., since 3.0) changed the <code id="mwBZA">/</code> operator to always represent floating-point division, e.g., <code class="nowrap mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt540" id="mwBZE" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"nowrap","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"5/2 == 2.5"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"class":{"wt":"nowrap"},"1":{"wt":"5/2 == 2.5"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="mi" id="mwBZI">5</span><span class="o" id="mwBZM">/</span><span class="mi" id="mwBZQ">2</span> <span class="o" id="mwBZU">==</span> <span class="mf" id="mwBZY">2.5</span></code>.</li>
<li id="mwBZc">The floor division <code id="mwBZg">//</code> operator was introduced, meaning that <code id="mwBZk">7//3 == 2</code>, <code id="mwBZo">-7//3 == -3</code>, <code id="mwBZs">7.5//3 == 2.0</code>, and <code id="mwBZw">-7.5//3 == -3.0</code>. For Python 2.7, adding the <code class="nowrap mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python2 mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt542" id="mwBZ0" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python2","class":"nowrap","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"from __future__ import division"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"class":{"wt":"nowrap"},"1":{"wt":"from __future__ import division"},"2":{"wt":"python2"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="kn" id="mwBZ4">from</span><span class="w" id="mwBZ8"> </span><span class="nn" id="mwBaA">__future__</span> <span class="kn" id="mwBaE">import</span> <span class="n" id="mwBaI">division</span></code> statement allows a module in Python 2.7 to use Python 3.x rules for division (see above).</li></ul>

<p id="mwBaM">In Python terms, the <code id="mwBaQ">/</code> operator represents <i id="mwBaU">true division</i> (or simply <i id="mwBaY">division</i>), while the <code id="mwBac">//</code> operator represents <i id="mwBag">floor division.</i> Before version 3.0, the <code id="mwBak">/</code> operator represents <i id="mwBao">classic division</i>.<sup about="#mwt544" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pep0238_121-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pep0238"}}'><a href="#cite_note-pep0238-121" id="mwBas"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBaw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBa0">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBa4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBa8"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding" title="Rounding" id="mwBbA">Rounding</a> towards negative infinity, though a different method than in most languages, adds consistency to Python. For instance, this rounding implies that the equation <code class="nowrap mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt545" id="mwBbE" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"nowrap","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"(a + b)//b == a//b + 1"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"class":{"wt":"nowrap"},"1":{"wt":"(a + b)//b == a//b + 1"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="p" id="mwBbI">(</span><span class="n" id="mwBbM">a</span> <span class="o" id="mwBbQ">+</span> <span class="n" id="mwBbU">b</span><span class="p" id="mwBbY">)</span><span class="o" id="mwBbc">//</span><span class="n" id="mwBbg">b</span> <span class="o" id="mwBbk">==</span> <span class="n" id="mwBbo">a</span><span class="o" id="mwBbs">//</span><span class="n" id="mwBbw">b</span> <span class="o" id="mwBb0">+</span> <span class="mi" id="mwBb4">1</span></code> is always true. Also, the rounding implies that the equation <code class="nowrap mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" style="" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt547" id="mwBb8" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","class":"nowrap","style":"","inline":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"b*(a//b) + a%b == a"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"code","href":"./Template:Code"},"params":{"class":{"wt":"nowrap"},"1":{"wt":"b*(a//b) + a%b == a"},"2":{"wt":"python"}},"i":0}}]}'><span class="n" id="mwBcA">b</span><span class="o" id="mwBcE">*</span><span class="p" id="mwBcI">(</span><span class="n" id="mwBcM">a</span><span class="o" id="mwBcQ">//</span><span class="n" id="mwBcU">b</span><span class="p" id="mwBcY">)</span> <span class="o" id="mwBcc">+</span> <span class="n" id="mwBcg">a</span><span class="o" id="mwBck">%</span><span class="n" id="mwBco">b</span> <span class="o" id="mwBcs">==</span> <span class="n" id="mwBcw">a</span></code> is valid for both positive and negative values of <code id="mwBc0">a</code>. As expected, the result of <code id="mwBc4">a%b</code> lies in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-open_interval" title="Half-open interval" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBc8">half-open interval</a> [0, <i id="mwBdA">b</i>), where <code id="mwBdE">b</code> is a positive integer; however, maintaining the validity of the equation requires that the result must lie in the interval (<i id="mwBdI">b</i>, 0] when <code id="mwBdM">b</code> is negative.<sup about="#mwt549" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-62_122-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-62"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-62-122" id="mwBdQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBdU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBdY">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBdc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBdg">Python provides a <code id="mwBdk">round</code> function for rounding a float to the nearest integer. For <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding#Tie-breaking" title="Rounding" id="mwBdo">tie-breaking</a>, Python<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwBds"> </span>3 uses the <i id="mwBdw">round to even</i> method: <code id="mwBd0">round(1.5)</code> and <code id="mwBd4">round(2.5)</code> both produce <code id="mwBd8">2</code>.<sup about="#mwt550" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-64_123-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-64"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-64-123" id="mwBeA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBeE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBeI">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBeM">]</span></span></a></sup> Python versions before 3 used the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding#Rounding_away_from_zero" title="Rounding" id="mwBeQ">round-away-from-zero</a> method: <code id="mwBeU">round(0.5)</code> is <code id="mwBeY">1.0</code>, and <code id="mwBec">round(-0.5)</code> is <code id="mwBeg">−1.0</code>.<sup about="#mwt551" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-63_124-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-63"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-63-124" id="mwBek"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBeo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBes">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBew">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBe0">Python allows Boolean expressions that contain multiple equality relations to be consistent with general usage in mathematics. For example, the expression <code id="mwBe4">a &lt; b &lt; c</code> tests whether <code id="mwBe8">a</code> is less than <code id="mwBfA">b</code> and <code id="mwBfE">b</code> is less than <code id="mwBfI">c</code>.<sup about="#mwt552" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-65_125-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-65"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-65-125" id="mwBfM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBfQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBfU">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBfY">]</span></span></a></sup> C-derived languages interpret this expression differently: in C, the expression would first evaluate <code id="mwBfc">a &lt; b</code>, resulting in 0 or 1, and that result would then be compared with <code id="mwBfg">c</code>.<sup about="#mwt553" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-CPL_126-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"CPL"}}'><a href="#cite_note-CPL-126" id="mwBfk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBfo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBfs">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBfw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBf0">Python uses <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary-precision_arithmetic" title="Arbitrary-precision arithmetic" id="mwBf4">arbitrary-precision arithmetic</a> for all integer operations. The <code id="mwBf8">Decimal</code> type/class in the <code id="mwBgA">decimal</code> module provides <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_floating_point" title="Decimal floating point" id="mwBgE">decimal floating-point numbers</a> to a pre-defined arbitrary precision with several rounding modes.<sup about="#mwt554" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-AutoNT-88_127-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"AutoNT-88"}}'><a href="#cite_note-AutoNT-88-127" id="mwBgI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBgM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBgQ">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBgU">]</span></span></a></sup> The <code id="mwBgY">Fraction</code> class in the <code id="mwBgc">fractions</code> module provides arbitrary precision for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number" title="Rational number" id="mwBgg">rational numbers</a>.<sup about="#mwt557" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-128" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-128"}}'><a href="#cite_note-128" id="mwBgk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBgo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBgs">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBgw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBg0">Due to Python's extensive mathematics library and the third-party library <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NumPy" title="NumPy" id="mwBg4">NumPy</a>, the language is frequently used for scientific scripting in tasks such as numerical data processing and manipulation.<sup about="#mwt560" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-129" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-129"}}'><a href="#cite_note-129" id="mwBg8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBhA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBhE">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBhI">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt563" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-130" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-130"}}'><a href="#cite_note-130" id="mwBhM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBhQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBhU">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBhY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="10" id="mwBhc" aria-labelledby="Function_syntax"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Function_syntax">Function syntax</h3></div>
<p id="mwBhg"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(computer_programming)" title="Function (computer programming)" id="mwBhk">Functions</a> are created in Python by using the <code id="mwBho">def</code> keyword. A function is defined similarly to how it is called, by first providing the function name and then the required parameters. Here is an example of a function that prints its inputs:</p>
<div class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python3 mw-content-ltr" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight" about="#mwt564" id="mwBhs" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python3"},"body":{"extsrc":"\ndef printer(input1, input2 = \"already there\"):\n    print(input1)\n    print(input2)\n\nprinter(\"hello\")\n\n# Example output:\n# hello\n# already there\n"}}'><pre id="mwBhw"><span id="mwBh0"></span><span class="k" id="mwBh4">def</span><span class="w" id="mwBh8"> </span><span class="nf" id="mwBiA">printer</span><span class="p" id="mwBiE">(</span><span class="n" id="mwBiI">input1</span><span class="p" id="mwBiM">,</span> <span class="n" id="mwBiQ">input2</span> <span class="o" id="mwBiU">=</span> <span class="s2" id="mwBiY">"already there"</span><span class="p" id="mwBic">):</span>
    <span class="nb" id="mwBig">print</span><span class="p" id="mwBik">(</span><span class="n" id="mwBio">input1</span><span class="p" id="mwBis">)</span>
    <span class="nb" id="mwBiw">print</span><span class="p" id="mwBi0">(</span><span class="n" id="mwBi4">input2</span><span class="p" id="mwBi8">)</span>

<span class="n" id="mwBjA">printer</span><span class="p" id="mwBjE">(</span><span class="s2" id="mwBjI">"hello"</span><span class="p" id="mwBjM">)</span>

<span class="c1" id="mwBjQ"># Example output:</span>
<span class="c1" id="mwBjU"># hello</span>
<span class="c1" id="mwBjY"># already there</span>
</pre></div><p id="mwBjc">To assign a default value to a function parameter in case no actual value is provided at run time, variable-definition syntax can be used inside the function header.</p>

<div class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight" about="#mwt565" id="mwBjs" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python"},"body":{"extsrc":"\nprint(&apos;Hello, World!&apos;)\n"}}'><pre id="mwBjw"><span id="mwBj0"></span><span class="nb" id="mwBj4">print</span><span class="p" id="mwBj8">(</span><span class="s1" id="mwBkA">'Hello, World!'</span><span class="p" id="mwBkE">)</span>
</pre></div>

<p id="mwBkI">Program to calculate the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factorial" title="Factorial" id="mwBkM">factorial</a> of a non-negative integer:</p>
<div class="mw-highlight mw-highlight-lang-python mw-content-ltr mw-highlight-lines" dir="ltr" typeof="mw:Extension/syntaxhighlight" about="#mwt566" id="mwBkQ" data-mw='{"name":"syntaxhighlight","attrs":{"lang":"python","line":"1"},"body":{"extsrc":"\ntext = input(&apos;Type a number, and its factorial will be printed: &apos;)\nn = int(text)\n\nif n &lt; 0:\n    raise ValueError(&apos;You must enter a non-negative integer&apos;)\n\nfactorial = 1\nfor i in range(2, n + 1):\n    factorial *= i\n\nprint(factorial)\n\n"}}'><pre id="mwBkU"><span id="mwBkY"></span><span class="linenos" data-line="1" id="mwBkc"></span><span class="n" id="mwBkg">text</span> <span class="o" id="mwBkk">=</span> <span class="nb" id="mwBko">input</span><span class="p" id="mwBks">(</span><span class="s1" id="mwBkw">'Type a number, and its factorial will be printed: '</span><span class="p" id="mwBk0">)</span>
